organic:oc-1xnyxrx.w: The alkene is Z. On each alkene carbon the methyl outranks the hydrogen, and the two methyls sit on the same side of the double bond.
s: On each alkene carbon, rank the two groups: **CH3 over H**.
Find the two higher-priority groups.
Both methyls are on the **same side**.
Same side is **Z** (zusammen, together).
t: R and S label stereocenters with four different groups. A double bond gets E or Z.
S is a label for a tetrahedral stereocenter, not for alkene geometry.
Each alkene carbon holds two different groups (CH3 and H), so geometric isomers do exist.
E means the higher-priority groups are on opposite sides. Here the methyls are on the same side.
c: Is cis-2-butene E or Z?
Z. For 2-butene, cis and Z mean the same thing.

originals:ab-c74e4a1474.w: A para nitro group. It pulls the phenoxide's negative charge onto its own oxygens by resonance, which stabilizes the anion and makes the phenol more acidic.
s: Remove the H: look at the **phenoxide**.
The charge reaches the **para carbon** by resonance.
A nitro group there takes the charge onto its **oxygens**.
More stable anion: **stronger acid**.
Donating groups (OCH3, NH2, CH3) push charge in and do the opposite.
c: Rough pKa of p-nitrophenol compared with phenol?
About 7 against about 10: roughly a thousand times more acidic.

organic:oc-15myqzk.w: The product is benzylamine. LiAlH4 turns an amide C=O into CH2 and keeps the carbon to nitrogen bond.
s: LiAlH4 is a strong **hydride** source.
Amides are reduced to **amines**.
The **C=O becomes CH2**; the oxygen is lost.
The nitrogen stays attached: C6H5CH2NH2.
t: Benzaldehyde has lost the nitrogen. LiAlH4 does not stop an amide at the aldehyde.
Benzyl alcohol is what an ester or acid gives. An amide keeps its nitrogen.
Aniline has lost the carbonyl carbon. That is the Hofmann rearrangement (Br2, NaOH), not a reduction.
Toluene has lost both the oxygen and the nitrogen. LiAlH4 removes only the oxygen.
c: What does LiAlH4 give with benzonitrile?
The same amine, benzylamine.

own-organic:ace-0003.w: A hydrogen moved with both of its bonding electrons (a hydride shift). Because it takes the pair along, the carbon it leaves becomes the positive one.
s: The cation carbon is short of electrons.
A neighboring **H moves over with its bonding pair**.
The carbon it left now lacks that pair: it is **positive**.
That carbon is tertiary: a more stable cation.
t: A bromide arriving would bond to the cation and end it. It would not move the charge to another carbon.
A positive charge on an sp3 carbon cannot drift by itself. Without a pi system, a group has to move.
A hydrogen with no electrons is a proton. If it left its pair behind, the carbon it left would be negative, not positive.
A migrating group always takes its bonding pair with it. That is what leaves the old carbon positive.
c: When does a methyl group shift instead of a hydrogen?
When the neighboring carbon has no hydrogen to give, as next to a quaternary carbon.

organic:oc-1jzd8nw.w: The only alkene is the one with the C=C between the old C-Cl carbon and the neighboring CH2 (2-menthene). E2 needs the H and the Cl anti to each other, both axial, and in the chair with Cl axial only the CH2 carbon has an axial H.
s: E2 needs H and Cl **anti-periplanar**: both axial on a ring.
Flip the chair so **Cl is axial**.
The H on the isopropyl carbon is then **equatorial**: unusable.
The CH2 on the other side has an **axial H**.
The C=C forms toward that CH2, away from the isopropyl carbon.
t: This is the more substituted alkene, at the isopropyl carbon. Its hydrogen cannot get anti to the chlorine.
An alcohol would be substitution. Ethoxide on a hindered secondary ring halide eliminates.
This puts a C=CH2 where the methyl was. That carbon is not next to the carbon holding Cl.
This is the alkane. Nothing here adds hydrogen.
c: Neomenthyl chloride has Cl axial in its stable chair. Which alkene does it give?
Mainly the more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene, and much faster, because an axial H is available on both sides.

organic:oc-ykycfl.w: Diethyl pimelate, the 1,7-diester. In a Dieckmann condensation the ring has one atom fewer than the chain, so seven carbons close to a six-membered ring.
s: The alpha carbon (C2) attacks the far ester carbon.
The ring holds C2 through the last carbon: **chain length minus one**.
Seven carbons: a **six-membered** ring.
Six carbons (adipate) give five; four (succinate) would give three.
t: Malonate has one carbon between its esters. There is nothing to close a ring with.
Oxalate has no alpha hydrogen at all, so it cannot form an enolate.
Succinate is the diester the stem says fails: closing it would make a three-membered ring.
Adipate closes to a five-membered ring, one atom short.
c: Which diester would you use for a five-membered beta-ketoester?
Diethyl adipate (the 1,6-diester).

organic:oc-1xtkdzx.w: Hot KMnO4, then acid. Vigorous permanganate oxidizes an alkyl side chain with a benzylic hydrogen down to a COOH on the ring.
s: The goal: side chain to **COOH** on the ring.
That is a strong **oxidation** at the benzylic carbon.
Hot KMnO4 does it when a **benzylic H** is present.
Acid workup turns the carboxylate into benzoic acid.
t: Cold dilute permanganate only adds two OH groups to alkenes. It is too mild to cut a side chain.
H2 with palladium is a reduction. It adds hydrogen and cannot make an acid.
Br2 with FeBr3 puts bromine on the ring. The side chain is untouched.
NaBH4 reduces aldehydes and ketones. It oxidizes nothing.
c: Would the same reagent convert tert-butylbenzene to benzoic acid?
No. tert-Butylbenzene has no benzylic hydrogen.

organic:oc-f00uzq.w: The 1,4-product is (E)-1-bromo-2-butene. The proton adds to an end carbon to give an allylic cation with charge on C2 and C4; bromide adds at C4, and the more stable trans alkene dominates.
s: H+ adds to **C1**: an allylic cation.
Resonance puts the charge on **C2 and C4**.
Bromide at C4 is **1,4-addition**; the C=C sits at C2 to C3.
That internal alkene is more substituted: the **thermodynamic** product.
Its more stable geometry is **E**.
t: 2-Bromobutane has no double bond left. One equivalent of HBr uses only one of the two C=C bonds.
3-Bromo-1-butene is the 1,2-product. It forms faster and dominates only at low temperature.
This is the Z isomer of the right compound. Under thermodynamic control the less crowded E alkene wins.
4-Bromo-1-butene would need H on an inner carbon and Br on the far end. The proton goes on an end carbon to make the allylic cation.
c: Which product dominates at low temperature?
The 1,2-product, 3-bromo-1-butene (kinetic control).

organic:oc-1bw83st.w: Bromine goes on the benzylic carbon, giving (2-bromopropan-2-yl)benzene. That hydrogen leaves a radical that is both tertiary and benzylic, the most stable one available.
s: NBS with light: **radical** bromination.
Cumene has one **benzylic H**, on the central carbon.
Removing it gives a tertiary, ring-stabilized radical.
Br ends up on that carbon.
t: Bromine para on the ring is aromatic substitution, which needs FeBr3.
A methyl hydrogen would leave a primary radical with no ring stabilization.
Bromine ortho on the ring also needs FeBr3, not radical conditions.
This has two bromines, one on the ring. The stem limits it to one, and ring bromination needs a Lewis acid.
c: Why is the benzylic radical so stable?
The unpaired electron is delocalized into the ring by resonance.

organic:oc-11y5yyy.w: The product is diethyl 2-oxobutanedioate: the CH2 of ethyl acetate ends up between a ketone that still carries its ester and its own ester. Diethyl oxalate has no alpha hydrogen, so it can only be attacked; the ethyl acetate enolate attacks it and ethoxide leaves.
s: Diethyl oxalate has **no alpha H**: electrophile only.
Ethoxide makes the **enolate** of ethyl acetate.
The enolate attacks one oxalate C=O.
**Ethoxide leaves**: a ketone flanked by two esters.
t: Ethyl acetoacetate comes from ethyl acetate reacting with itself. The oxalate carbonyl is the more reactive electrophile, so the crossed product wins.
This has an aldehyde where an ester should be. Nothing here reduces an ester.
This has an OH where the ketone should be. A Claisen condensation expels ethoxide and keeps the C=O.
This has five carbons in its backbone. Two from oxalate and two from acetate make four.
c: Why does a crossed Claisen work cleanly with diethyl oxalate?
Only one partner can form an enolate, so only one crossed product is possible.

organic:oc-4hs54s.w: Transesterification. One ester is converted into another by exchanging its OCH3 for OCH2CH3, with acid catalysis and excess ethanol to push the equilibrium.
s: Start: an **ester**. Finish: a different **ester**.
Only the **alkoxy group** changed.
Swapping the OR of an ester is **transesterification**.
Excess ethanol drives the equilibrium forward.
t: Fischer esterification starts from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. This starts from an ester.
Hydrolysis uses water and gives the carboxylic acid. Here the product is another ester.
Saponification is ester hydrolysis with hydroxide and gives a carboxylate salt.
A Claisen condensation joins two esters through carbon to make a beta-keto ester.
c: What is the nucleophile in this reaction?
Ethanol. It attacks the protonated ester carbonyl.

organic:oc-1ix28dz.w: Bromide attacks a carbon of the bromonium ion from the side opposite the bridging bromine, so the two bromines end up trans. The bridge blocks one face, which is why the addition is anti.
s: The alkene attacks Br2: a three-membered **bromonium** ion.
The bridging Br **blocks one face**.
Bromide attacks a ring carbon from the **opposite face**.
The bridge opens: the two Br are **trans** (anti addition).
t: The bridge occupies that face, so bromide cannot come in there. Same-face attack would give cis, which is not seen.
The second bromine does not arrive in the same step as the first, and the product is trans, not cis.
No open cation forms. The bridging bromine holds the geometry, which is why only the trans product appears.
The arrow runs the wrong way: bromide is the nucleophile, and it attacks carbon. No monobromide forms.
c: Is the trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane product optically active?
No. It forms as a racemic mixture of the two trans enantiomers.

organic:oc-jr6ldy.w: The product is the fused bicyclic with a new cyclohexene ring, with the quinone's other C=C and both C=O groups unchanged. Butadiene adds across one C=C of the quinone, which is the dienophile.
s: Butadiene is the **diene**; one quinone C=C is the **dienophile**.
Two new sigma bonds close a **cyclohexene** ring.
The new C=C sits in the middle of the old diene.
The quinone's **other C=C** and both C=O are untouched.
t: This shows the two starting pieces with nothing joined. p-Benzoquinone is a very good dienophile and does react.
Here the quinone's second C=C has been lost too. One equivalent of diene uses only one of them.
This is the enol form with two OH groups on an aromatic ring. The first-formed adduct is the diketone.
A fully aromatic naphthoquinone has lost four hydrogens. That would need a separate oxidation.
c: Why is p-benzoquinone such a good dienophile?
Each C=C has an electron-withdrawing C=O on both sides, which makes it electron-poor.

organic:oc-7d9eh6.w: The product is cyclohexanol. As bromide leaves, a ring bond migrates so the five-membered ring grows to six and the charge sits on a ring carbon (secondary); water then adds there.
s: Bromide leaves: the charge starts on the **CH2 outside the ring**.
A ring C-C bond migrates to it: **ring expansion**.
Now a six-membered ring with a **secondary** cation.
Water adds and loses H+: **cyclohexanol**.
t: 1-Methylcyclopentene is an alkene. The stem says the major product is an alcohol.
Cyclohexene has the expanded ring but is the elimination product, not the alcohol.
Cyclopentylmethanol is the unrearranged product. It would need a primary cation or SN2 at a hindered carbon.
Methylenecyclopentane is an unrearranged alkene, not an alcohol.
c: What drives this rearrangement?
A primary cation becomes secondary, and a five-membered ring becomes a nearly strain-free six.

organic:oc-1miej84.w: tert-Butanol, by Markovnikov addition. The proton adds to the CH2 carbon to give the tertiary cation, and water bonds to the central carbon.
s: H+ adds to the **CH2** carbon.
That leaves a **tertiary** cation on the central carbon.
Water attacks the cation.
Loss of H+ gives **tert-butanol**.
t: An epoxide needs a peroxyacid such as mCPBA. Dilute acid adds water.
A diol needs an oxidant such as OsO4 or cold KMnO4. Dilute sulfuric acid is not one.
Reduction to the alkane needs H2 and a metal catalyst.
The primary alcohol is the anti-Markovnikov product. That takes hydroboration-oxidation.
c: Which reagents give 2-methylpropan-1-ol from this alkene?
BH3-THF, then H2O2 and NaOH.
